studies.title: Aave V3 liquidations on Arbitrum One, 30 days (2026-10-24 to 2026-11-25, real data)

blocks.text: Produced by npm run liquidations -- --days 30 --logs-rpc-url https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc --sample-hf 60 on the owner's machine, read-only (2,024 RPC calls, 0 retries). Logs came from the public Arbitrum RPC, prices and borrower states from a free Alchemy RPC. Everything from "Per day" to "Limitations" is the tool's output, pasted unedited; the section "Reading it (analyst notes)" at the end is mine and is labelled as such.

items: Aave V3 Pool: 0x794a61358D6845594F94dc1DB02A252b5b4814aD (verified on-chain by scripts/verify-addresses.sh)
Liquidation events found: 1031
Log scan: 177 getLogs requests, 0 range errors, final chunk 50000 blocks

blocks.text: Per day (UTC)

Size: median $264, 90th percentile $5,792. Bonus measured at oracle prices: median 4.50%, 10th–90th percentile 4.50%–6.30% (gross of Aave's protocol fee on the bonus, so what a liquidator keeps is a bit lower).
How big is the prize? (gross bonus per liquidation, before swap costs, gas and loan fees)
Whole market, all liquidators together: gross bonus of $155,363 over about 30.0 day(s) (about $5,179 per day) before swap costs, gas and loan fees; the 3 largest liquidations made up 16% of it.
Assets
Who liquidates
54 distinct liquidator address(es); the top 3 took 73% of all liquidations.
How fast are liquidations taken? (sample)

For 73 sampled liquidations the borrower's health factor was read at past blocks (state at the end of each block) to find the first block from which the position stayed liquidatable (health factor < 1) until it was liquidated. "0 blocks" means it became liquidatable inside the liquidation block itself (typically an oracle price update followed by the bot in the same block). On Arbitrum one block is about 0.25 s.

rows: Liquidations not sampled: same borrower already liquidated within 20000 blocks (partial liquidations)
Failed to read (RPC error / archive state unavailable)
Still liquidatable at the 20000-block lookback limit (delay is a lower bound)

blocks.text: Speed by prize size (clean samples)
Verdict: CROWDED

81% of the sampled liquidations (73 clean samples) happened within 2 block(s) of the position becoming liquidatable (median 0 block(s), 74% in the very same block). 54 distinct liquidator address(es) in the period, the top 3 took 73% of all liquidations. Weighted by gross bonus, 100% of the sampled prize was taken within 2 blocks. 13 sampled liquidation(s) waited more than 10 blocks; their median gross bonus was $0.02 against $56.00 for the instant ones, and together they carry 0% of the sampled gross bonus (the slow ones are the small ones: positions too small to pay for gas and swaps may simply be left alone). Professional bots take essentially every liquidation worth taking immediately, usually in the same block as the price update that triggers it. A bot running on a free RPC and a laptop cannot realistically be first. Treat a liquidation bot as a portfolio project, not a profit source.
Rule used: "crowded" when at least 70% of clean samples are within 2 blocks and there are at least 10 samples. These thresholds are my rule of thumb, not a law.
Limitations

items: The delay is measured on a sample of liquidations, and with the borrower's state at block granularity; it cannot see transactions that were sent but lost the race.
A liquidation that happens in the very same block as the price update shows as 0 blocks: it proves the liquidator reacted immediately, not who it was.
Prices come from the oracle currently registered in the Aave address provider, queried at each event's block; events from before that oracle existed have no price.
"Gross bonus" ignores the cost of swapping the collateral back, gas and any flash-loan fee, so it overstates what a bot would keep.
This is a measurement of the past; it says nothing about positions that will become liquidatable tomorrow.

blocks.text: Reading it (analyst notes, not tool output)

items: The prize comes in bursts. Seven days (Nov 8, 10, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21) produced $144,353 of the month's $155,363 gross bonus (92.9%, summed from the per-day table above). The first 3-day report (about $122/day) happened to cover calm days only, which is why a longer window mattered.

Speed does not depend on luck, it depends on size. Every sampled liquidation with a gross bonus of $1 or more was taken within 2 blocks, except one in the $20–$100 bucket that was still liquidatable at the 20,000-block lookback limit. That single case is worth inspecting individually (asset pair, liquidity of the collateral) but one case is not an opening.
Concentrated competition. One address took 39% of the liquidations and repaid $1.66M of debt; the top 3 took 73%.

Conclusion. Liquidations on Aave V3 Arbitrum are a real market (about $155k of gross bonus in 30 days) but every liquidation worth taking is taken in the same block as the price update. A free-RPC laptop bot would not be first; a liquidation module in this project is a portfolio piece, not a profit source.

blocks.text: Addendum: focus on the hard-to-source debt assets (LUSD, EURS)

Run on the same 30-day range with --focus-debt LUSD,EURS (18 extra liquidations measured besides the random sample). These measurements are kept out of the verdict above. Table pasted unedited from the tool's output:
Reading it (analyst notes, not tool output)

items: The hypothesis is supported in direction. Liquidations with these debt assets wait much longer than the rest: 53% (LUSD) and 17% (EURS) were taken within 2 blocks, against 81% overall and 100% of those with a gross bonus of $1 or more. EURS had a median wait of 1,086 blocks (about 5 minutes). Most of the money of these two assets sat in the slow liquidations: $194.26 of $272.31 (71%) for LUSD and $11.58 of $15.21 (76%) for EURS.

But the whole niche is tiny. All 65 liquidations of both assets paid $287.52 of gross bonus in 30 days (about $9.6 a day); the part that waited more than 10 blocks was $205.84 (about $6.9 a day), before gas, swap costs and any financing.

Most events were not measured. 28 of 43 LUSD and 16 of 22 EURS liquidations are repeats (the same borrower liquidated again within 20,000 blocks, i.e. a series of partial liquidations), which the delay measurement skips because the position stays liquidatable between them by definition. So the table describes the first liquidation of each series (15 and 6 cases).

Getting the debt asset is the real obstacle. The zero-interest lenders used by this project were not checked for LUSD or EURS and are unlikely to hold them in size; a liquidator would have to buy the asset first, with slippage, which the gross bonus figures above do not include.

Conclusion. The slow liquidations are real and are concentrated in hard-to-source debt assets, but they are worth about $7 a day gross in total. This does not change the verdict: a liquidation bot here is a portfolio project, not a profit source.

studies.title: Backtest report: Arbitrum One, ~24 hours of real data

blocks.text: Produced on 2026-11-24 with npm run collect + npm run backtest on the author's machine (Ubuntu on WSL2, free Alchemy RPC). The table below is the tool's output, pasted unedited.

items: Data source: rpc-archive (real on-chain quotes: Uniswap QuoterV2 / SushiSwap getAmountsOut, recorded per block)
Snapshots replayed: 48 (blocks 526627702–526966102), one every 7,200 blocks (about 30 minutes), 26 price curves each
Measured gas price during the window: about 0.020 gwei
Collection time: 32 minutes on the free tier (about 40 s per snapshot)
Config at the time: trade sizes $1k / $5k / $25k (the $100k size is above the $50k risk cap), Aave premium 5 bps, slippage reserve 10 bps, minimum net profit $1

blocks.text: Reading it

items: No profitable opportunity in 2,976 evaluated routes. Every round trip lost money once the flash-loan premium, DEX fees, price impact, slippage reserve and gas were counted.

feeTier came closest (best route about $2.51 short of break-even), then triangular, then crossDex. The SushiSwap legs of crossDex routes suffer from thinner liquidity on Arbitrum, so price impact dominates.
A 3-snapshot pilot run the same day showed the same ordering (-4.03 / -17.23 / -66.35).

blocks.text: Limitations

items: Snapshots are taken every ~30 minutes. Gaps that open and close within seconds (which is where real arbitrage lives, and where faster bots compete) are invisible to this sampling. "Zero" here means "none that persisted at sample time".
Results are an upper bound: fills at the recorded quote, no competing bots, no latency.
newPoolScanner cannot be backtested with this dataset format.
One day of data, a fixed set of 13 pairs/venues, and fixed trade sizes.

blocks.text: Re-run with a zero-fee lender (Balancer V2 Vault)
Same 48 snapshots, replayed with --flash-fee-bps 0 (the Balancer V2 Vault charged no flash-loan fee on Arbitrum when checked on-chain on 2026-11-24). Output pasted unedited:

items: Flash-loan fee assumed: 0 bps (Balancer V2 Vault, zero fee)

blocks.text: Every "closest to break-even" value improved by exactly $0.50, which is the 5 bps Aave premium on a $1,000 trade: the routes that came closest were all at the smallest trade size. Removing the loan fee did not make any route profitable.

Why: on the closest route (WETH -> USDC on the 0.05% pool, back on the 0.30% pool), the two pool fees alone cost about 0.35% of the trade. Arbitrage keeps the price gap between two pools inside that fee band, so a sample taken at a random moment almost always finds a gap smaller than the fees. Profit exists only in the short moment right after a large swap pushes a pool outside the band, and it goes to whoever acts first.

studies.title: Gap monitor report: expanded radar, one hour of Arbitrum One (2026-11-24)

blocks.text: npm run monitor -- --minutes 60 --interval-ms 500 with radar.config.json (Uniswap V3 0.01/0.05/0.3/1% tiers, PancakeSwap V3, SushiSwap; 10 tokens). Table transcribed from a screenshot of the tool's output; only rows with at least one episode are listed in full. Zero-interest lenders: WETH (Balancer V2 / Uniswap V4), USDC (Uniswap V4). Net = exact on-chain quote at that block (DEX fees and price impact included) - 10 bps safety reserve - estimated gas.

items: Blocks: 527214753–527227051 (12,299 blocks), 6,855 polls every 500 ms, 0 errors
Pools: 29 used of 91 found (pools under $50,000 TVL skipped as dead); pool pairs compared: 32

blocks.text: The other 20 pool pairs never left their fee band (max excess between -1 and -70.3 bps), including USDC/USDT across Uniswap and PancakeSwap, WBTC/WETH and WBTC/USDC across tiers, and LINK/WETH.
Reading it

items: Much closer to break-even than before. Across 32 pool pairs and 11 with episodes, the best estimated nets were between -$0.12 and -$0.47 (one ARB/USDC outlier at -$3.09), versus -$2.09 / -$84.91 in the first radar hour.

The standout: WETH/USDC between the Uniswap 0.01% and PancakeSwap 0.01% pools was outside its (2 bps) fee band 64% of the time, in 50 episodes, median ~23 s and up to ~2.7 min, with excess up to 10 bps over the band.
Still no episode with a positive net under these assumptions. The 10 bps safety reserve is of the same size as the remaining gap; see the follow-up run that reports the net before the reserve.

studies.title: Gap monitor report: one hour of Arbitrum One (2026-11-24)

blocks.text: Produced with npm run monitor -- --minutes 60 --interval-ms 500 on the author's machine (free Alchemy RPC). One eth_call (Multicall3) per poll; block numbers are Arbitrum L2 blocks (about 0.25 s each). The table is the tool's output, pasted unedited. Lender: Balancer V2 (zero-interest), so only WETH is borrowable; "(hyp.)" marks a quote that would need a token the lender cannot supply.

items: Blocks: 527184943–527197622 (12680 blocks), 6893 polls every 500 ms, 0 errors
Trade sizes quoted when a gap opened: $100, $250, $500, $1000, $5000

blocks.text: Reading it

items: Deep pools never left the fee band (Uniswap tier vs Uniswap tier, all hour, at 2-block resolution).

Gaps that did leave the band were in thin pools. The SushiSwap ARB/USDC pool sat 70 bps outside the band for ~50 minutes, yet the best quote lost $84.91: the pool is close to empty, so its "price" is stale and any trade moves it. The SushiSwap WETH/USDC and WETH/USDT gaps (up to ~13 bps, lasting up to ~90 s) also quoted negative after price impact.
In short: where there is liquidity there is no gap, and where there is a gap there is not enough liquidity to profit.
Limits: polls every 500 ms (about one block in two); quotes are taken when an episode opens, not at its peak; 13 pool pairs on 3 venues only.

studies.title: Gap monitor report: expanded radar with "net before safety reserve" (2026-11-24)

blocks.text: Same setup as the expanded run (29 alive pools of 91, 32 pool pairs, zero-interest lenders), with two extra columns: the trade size of the best quote, and the best net before the 10 bps slippage safety reserve (the quote itself is an exact on-chain quote at that block, fees and price impact included). Output pasted unedited (rows with episodes only).

items: Blocks: 527228609–527240071 (11,463 blocks), 5,608 polls every 500 ms, 1 error

blocks.text: The other 24 pool pairs never left their fee band (max excess from -1.7 to -102.4 bps).
Reading it

items: Still no positive episode, even without the safety reserve. Best: -$0.02 (WBTC/WETH), then -$0.08.

The best size was always the smallest ($100). Larger trades lose more to price impact. With gaps of at most ~9.5 bps over the fee band, the gross edge on $100 is a few cents, about the same as gas (~$0.04 estimated). That is why these gaps can stay open for tens of seconds: nobody takes them because they are not worth taking.

Conclusion after three hours of block-level monitoring on 91 pools across Uniswap V3, PancakeSwap V3 and SushiSwap, with zero-interest loans: two-pool arbitrage on these mainstream Arbitrum pairs did not produce a single profitable opportunity for a bot running on free infrastructure. The best case was within a few cents of break-even.
